title: Songs in the hospital and singing Cock Robin
summary: Asked whether he misses singing in hospital, Punch sings Cock Robin; the interviewers recall an earlier visitor.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: Do you miss singing now here in the hospital? Here in the hospital, do you miss singing? Do you...
Do you think of writing songs? Or is there something when you're lying in bed?
Well, no, I haven't sung it this time. I just think I'm getting out of here.
Why don't you write a song called Cock Robin? That'll make a good song, wouldn't it, Paul? Oh, yeah. He has. I like that number. Yeah.
How do the words to that work?
You don't have to sing it. But what is it about being in the... Well, I have to sing... In the winter, in the cold?
I have to sing it to get straight.
Oh, well, don't sing it. Don't strain your voice.

One day the sun was warm and bright, no clouds seen in the sky. Miss Robin said to the little one, it's time you all should fly. And every little Robin said to Mom, I'll try, I'll try, I'll try. Sure I know the child and the good one, so I'll try.

Tell you all by and by. But you got to fly, fly, fly, fly. Every little one got to fly high. Fly, fly, fly high. Before mother die. It was well as winter when time was rough. I was in the weather strutting my stuff. So fly, fly, fly, fly. Every little one got to fly high.

I knew she'd get a kick out of that. You remember when that girl came around to see you? Her name was Irish Turner Kelso in the hospital. We got a nice interview and you sang that song. She's from Mississippi. Her cousin was editor of the New York Times. That's what I'm trying to say. You see her on the TV now. Them guys late too. That's her. She's the one who called you.
